title: Reverse engineering trading strategy
author: Altruistic_Winter909
selftext: I have somone who is strategie 90% successful and i want to know how he doing it i have his data **(**the price he entered and price of tp and the stop loses **)** i have more than 200 data does anyone have а idea to know his strategy?

comments.author: Scott_Malkinsons
comments.body:
If he has a 90% win rate, the strategy is risk more than you win. Win rate has an inverse correlation with risk:reward, so if you want a 90% win rate just run a 4:1 risk reward with a slight edge (since you're starting with 80% odds).

If the TP and SL is like 1:1 risk:reward or better then the person is, most likely, to be full of it and posting fake numbers. Does this person post live? Because anything other than live is total BS. Statements, etc. mean nothing because I can have 10 accounts, 9 that lose money, and only show you the one account that got lucky. If the trader isn't posting live, don't believe a word they say.

Can you tell the entire strat with just entry, tp, and sl? Maybe. If they're using off the shelf indicators you can sometimes cross reference it.

comments.author: Yoksel_algo
comments.body:
Let's be realistic: trying to reverse engineer a black-box strategy based solely on execution logs (entries, TP, SL) without a rigorous framework is pure guesswork. In quantitative trading, guesswork always leads to curve-fitting, which guarantees a blown account the moment the market regime shifts. 

An alleged 90% win rate with a 1:3 risk-to-reward on XAUUSD implies the underlying strategy is exploiting highly specific liquidity pools or micro-structural inefficiencies. To actually decode this without falling into a data-artifact trap, you must avoid looking at entries in isolation and instead reconstruct the exact structural context across three layers:

* 1. Multi-Timeframe Alignment: You need to identify the exact analytical timeframes being used. A strategy executing on a 1-minute chart is almost certainly reacting to key liquidity pools or structural shifts identified on the 15-minute or 1-hour higher timeframe (HTF). Without aligning execution to the HTF context, the data points will look completely random.

* 2. The Distribution Methodology: Since you mentioned ICT concepts, the core of the strategy relies on understanding the specific algorithm of order delivery and distribution (e.g., premium vs. discount arrays, accumulation/manipulation/distribution cycles). You must evaluate whether the entries occur during specific liquidity sweeps or fixed time-of-day windows (Killzones).

* 3. Continuous Microstructure Tracking: You need a mechanism to track the market state continuously across the entire timeline of all 200+ trades. Instead of just analyzing the moments of entry and exit, you have to monitor the order flow, delta distributions, and volume profiles before, during, and after execution to see what actually triggers the logic.

When we designed the analytical framework for ii-nt.net, we found that trying to reverse engineer logic without decoupling these layers always leads to massive hallucinations. If you don't bound the search space by timeframe alignment and distribution mechanics, the system will just find fake correlations that look great on historical logs but fail completely on the next live trade.
